about: Planted cards for the card check (decision 2.26), like the judge's planted picks: each is clearly honest or clearly wrong against the book's catalog facts, for a real reader in profile-v1. Written Nov 8, before the check was run on them. 'subtle' items test the hard part: claims about how a book feels.

items.title: A Psalm for the Wild-Built
items.author: Becky Chambers
items.why: Accurate: a gentle, hopeful novella about a tea monk and a robot.

card.hook: A tea monk and a curious robot walk into the wilderness.
card.why: This is the quiet, hopeful comfort read you're after: a wandering tea monk meets a robot, and they talk about what people need. It's short, gentle and warm all the way through.
card.angleText: Its conversations about purpose and rest are light on plot and heavy on warmth, which makes it easy to sink into.

items.title: A Psalm for the Wild-Built
items.author: Becky Chambers
items.why: Wrong feel and plot: it is not a violent survival thriller.

card.hook: Survival is a war, and the robots are winning.
card.why: A brutal survival thriller in which a monk fights off killer robots across a ruined wasteland. Relentless and bloody from the first page.
card.angleText: Its battle scenes are the most violent in recent science fiction.

items.title: We Have Always Lived in the Castle
items.author: Shirley Jackson
items.why: Accurate, including a warranted heads-up about the horror shelving.

card.hook: Two sisters, one house, and a village that hates them.
card.why: An isolated family, hostile neighbours and a narrator whose calm makes everything stranger. It's sometimes shelved with horror, but its menace is quiet and psychological.
card.angleText: The dread builds through voice and atmosphere rather than shocks.

items.title: We Have Always Lived in the Castle
items.author: Shirley Jackson
items.why: Wrong: no slasher, gore or jump scares.

card.hook: A slasher in a country house.
card.why: A gory slasher packed with jump scares, as a masked killer stalks two sisters through their house night after night.
card.angleText: Its kills are graphic and frequent.

items.title: The Wild Robot
items.author: Peter Brown
items.why: Accurate: a robot learns to survive on a wild island and raises a gosling.

card.hook: A robot washes up on an island full of animals.
card.why: Roz the robot learns to survive in the wild and becomes a mother to an orphaned gosling, in short chapters made for reading aloud.
card.angleText: It's warm and funny, with an adventure that kids can follow chapter by chapter.

items.title: The Wild Robot
items.author: Peter Brown
items.why: Wrong audience and feel: not a dark dystopia for adults.

card.hook: Humanity's last war, told by a machine.
card.why: A bleak adult dystopia about robots exterminating the last humans, full of despair and graphic violence.
card.angleText: It's one of the darkest novels of the decade, written for grown readers only.

items.title: Three Men in a Boat
items.author: Jerome K. Jerome
items.why: Accurate: a comic account of a boating holiday on the Thames.

card.hook: Three friends, one dog and a boat on the Thames.
card.why: A short, very funny classic: three friends and a dog take a boating holiday on the Thames, and almost everything goes comically wrong.
card.angleText: Its digressions and mishaps still make readers laugh out loud.

items.title: Three Men in a Boat
items.author: Jerome K. Jerome
items.why: Wrong: not a tragic war story.

card.hook: Three soldiers who never came home.
card.why: A tense, tragic story of three soldiers trapped behind enemy lines, unflinching about the horrors of war.

items.title: The Employees
items.author: Olga Ravn
items.why: Feel contradicted: the catalog calls it funny and tags it funny; the card says it isn't.

card.hook: Testimonies from a ship's crew, human and not.
card.why: It has the eerie corporate remove that made Severance unsettling, told through a crew's workplace testimonies. It's melancholy and solemn throughout, with no humour at all.
card.angleText: Its fragmented statements build a quiet, humourless dread.

items.title: The Employees
items.author: Olga Ravn
items.why: Feel matches: funny and doom-laden, as the catalog says.

card.hook: Testimonies from a ship's crew, human and not.
card.why: It has the uncanny workplace dread that drew you to Severance, told through a crew's testimonies to a corporate committee, and it's darkly funny along the way.
card.angleText: Its fragmented statements are both unsettling and wry.

items.title: A Kiss Before Dying
items.author: Ira Levin
items.why: Feel contradicted: the card calls it light and cosy; it's a dark murder story.

card.hook: An ambitious young man courts a rich family.
card.why: A light, cosy read with nothing grim in it: an ambitious young man courts a wealthy family's daughters, and the twists stay playful.
card.angleText: It's the gentlest of thrillers, perfect if you want less bleak.

items.title: A Kiss Before Dying
items.author: Ira Levin
items.why: Accurate, and honest that it is dark rather than claiming 'less bleak'.

card.hook: An ambitious young man will do anything to marry money.
card.why: A tightly plotted suspense novel told partly from inside a ruthless schemer's head, with twists that keep rearranging what you know. It's dark, so it won't soften the edges much.
card.angleText: Its structure hides the killer's identity in plain sight.
